problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$

feedback.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}} & =L{{e}^{5t}}+L{-{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{5t}}-L{{e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5},\,s>5 \\ L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{5t}}-L{{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-5}-\frac{1}{s-2} \\  & =\frac{(s-2)-(s-5)}{(s-5)(s-2)} \\  & =\frac{s-2-s+5}{(s-5)(s-2)} \\  & =\frac{3}{(s-5)(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (2,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(5,\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=(5,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>5.$
